slides.title: A fault is a request for a decision, not always a disaster
keyPoints: Translation could not complete the requested access
The kernel checks the region’s logical policy
Recovery and rejection are both possible results
slides.narration: A page fault means the attempted memory access could not complete under the current translation or protection state. That can be part of normal demand paging, or it can reveal an invalid operation. The kernel must determine the address, requested access, and mapping policy before choosing recovery. A valid anonymous page may receive zero-filled backing; a forbidden write may be rejected. It is therefore misleading to say every page fault means a crash or every page fault means a disk read. Our programs safely model these policy choices without deliberately dereferencing invalid memory or trying to recover from corrupted application state.

slides.title: Classify before allocating
keyPoints: The model separates logical region policy from presence
Read-only writes are denied
Anonymous absence and copy-on-write need different work
slides.narration: The program asks four policy questions without accessing any page. An absent anonymous region yields demand-zero. A write to a read-only region yields deny. A write to a copy-on-write region yields private-write, while a read of a present read-only region can resume. The printed words are decisions in a simplified function, not proof that a kernel allocated memory or raised an exception. The order matters: an invalid region must not be granted storage merely because it lacks a present page. A real handler has more states and synchronization duties, but it preserves the same distinction between logical permission and current backing.

slides.title: Demand-zero need not involve a storage device
keyPoints: Anonymous memory promises initialized zero bytes
Backing may be supplied on first use
Fault counts alone do not measure I/O
slides.narration: A program can reserve anonymous memory without touching every page. When it first accesses a legitimate page, the kernel can supply zero-initialized backing according to the mapping contract. No existing file contents need to be read for that demand-zero case. A file-backed fault is different, and even then the required data may already be in the operating system’s cache. Counting all faults together therefore mixes operations with very different costs. When a workload gets slower, distinguish fault type, amount of backing work, and storage waiting before blaming the device. The same number of page faults can correspond to very different elapsed time.

slides.title: Private writing copies only the model page that needs separation
keyPoints: Two owners initially share two model pages
First write detaches one page
A later write to the exclusive page needs no second copy
slides.narration: Our page objects contain two integers each. Parent and child initially share both objects. The first child write to page zero sees another owner and creates a private copy. A second write to that same page changes the exclusive copy without another allocation, leaving the copy counter at one. The final output is parent seven, child eleven, copies one; the untouched second page remains shared. This is an ownership model in one C++ process, not an actual fork or hardware page fault. It illustrates the private-modification guarantee and why one should not promise that every later write requires a new physical copy.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Prepare private backing first, then write it. Keep the thread-safety and lifetime assumptions explicit.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
keyPoints: Copying the old value before assignment preserves the private-write contract. If allocation throws, the assignment to owner has not yet committed and the original shared value remains intact. unique() is suitable only under this lab’s single-threaded access rule; it does not establish a safe concurrent mutation protocol. OS copy-on-write applies similar intent at a different boundary.
A plausible alternative: Eager copying is simpler when data is small or almost every element will change.

slides.title: Missing pages
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A missing translation can correspond to a legitimate region whose physical backing has not yet been installed.
Anonymous memory can be provided lazily, and file-backed mappings can bring in pages as needed.
Deferring work avoids allocating and reading pages that the application never touches.
A missing page can also correspond to no valid mapping at all.
slides.narration:
A missing translation can correspond to a legitimate region whose physical backing has not yet been installed. Anonymous memory can be provided lazily, and file-backed mappings can bring in pages as needed. Deferring work avoids allocating and reading pages that the application never touches. A missing page can also correspond to no valid mapping at all. The handler must consult the mapping policy rather than assume that any requested address deserves storage. Otherwise, invalid pointers would silently create new memory instead of being rejected.

In plain English: The program uses a map of memory addresses. The operating system translates that map to where the data is actually stored.

slides.title: Protection faults
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A protection fault occurs when a mapping exists or is described, but the attempted operation is not permitted by the active protection state.
Writing to a read-only mapping and fetching instructions from a non-executable mapping are examples under the relevant hardware configuration.
Some protection faults are intentionally recoverable, notably copy-on-write.
Others indicate an error.
slides.narration: A protection fault occurs when a mapping exists or is described, but the attempted operation is not permitted by the active protection state. Writing to a read-only mapping and fetching instructions from a non-executable mapping are examples under the relevant hardware configuration. Some protection faults are intentionally recoverable, notably copy-on-write. Others indicate an error. The handler must distinguish the region’s logical policy from its current hardware permission bits. A read-only code page is not made writable simply because a process attempted a store.

slides.title: Copy-on-write
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Copy-on-write lets logically independent mappings share backing until a writer requires a private version.
After fork , parent and child can initially share many physical pages while observing private-memory semantics.
A write fault can cause the kernel to create a private copy for the writer and update its mapping. [ R15 ]
A physical copy is not mandatory in every write-fault case.
slides.narration: Copy-on-write lets logically independent mappings share backing until a writer requires a private version. After fork , parent and child can initially share many physical pages while observing private-memory semantics. A write fault can cause the kernel to create a private copy for the writer and update its mapping. [ R15 ] A physical copy is not mandatory in every write-fault case. If the kernel determines that the backing is no longer shared in a way requiring separation, it may be able to make the page writable without copying. The semantic guarantee is private modification, not a promise that every store invokes a particular copying algorithm.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The following model uses immutable Python bytes as initial shared content and returns a new object when a private writer changes a byte.

Companion listing: ch26/cow_model.py
The expected output is ABCD AXCD .
slides.narration: The following model uses immutable Python bytes as initial shared content and returns a new object when a private writer changes a byte. It demonstrates the observable contract of copy-on-write; it does not claim to implement page tables or reproduce the kernel’s physical allocation decisions. Companion listing: ch26/cow_model.py The expected output is ABCD AXCD . The model copies the entire small object for every store, which is deliberately simpler than a page-based implementation. Its value is that the ownership and visibility contract can be checked without relying on process scheduling or privileged inspection. The model also clarifies a boundary: a shared mapping would require a different contract. Making a private copy is correct for private modification but wrong for a communication region whose purpose is to expose one participant’s writes to another.

slides.title: Copy-on-write separates logical permission from the current hardware bit
keyPoints: A logically writable private region may be temporarily read-only
A write can trigger private backing preparation
Truly read-only code must remain protected
slides.narration: A copy-on-write region may be logically allowed to change even though its current hardware mapping denies a direct store. That temporary protection lets the kernel intervene when a private version becomes necessary. A permanently read-only code mapping can use a similar-looking protection bit but has a different policy: a write is an error. The handler therefore needs more than the leaf writable bit to decide what recovery is allowed. Our classification program uses an explicit region kind to make that missing policy visible. Real kernels maintain richer metadata and coordinate it with mappings and other threads.
actions: Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

question.prompt: Why can the same kind of hardware write fault lead to either recovery or rejection?
question.answer: The region’s logical policy may allow private modification or may forbid writing entirely.

slides.title: Resume only after the required invariant is restored
keyPoints: Validate the requested access
Obtain appropriate backing and update translation state
Retry or reject the faulting operation according to the platform
slides.narration: The conceptual recovery path checks policy, obtains suitable backing, updates translation information, and then allows the operation to resume when permitted. Each step establishes a condition needed by the next. Resuming too early would repeat the unresolved access or expose wrong storage. Rejecting an invalid access is not a failure of demand paging; it is enforcement of the boundary. Real implementations also handle concurrent mapping changes and several threads faulting on related storage. Our models intentionally omit those races. A function that returns a policy word does not claim to perform page-table updates, translation invalidation, or instruction restart.
actions: Ask for the concrete state change or units before revealing the explanation.

question.prompt: Why is returning from a handler without fixing a recoverable mapping insufficient?
question.answer: The original access still lacks the required translation or permission, so the recovery invariant has not been established.

keyPoints: Check object and buffer contracts before access
Use return codes for expected resource errors
A fault may leave application state unsafe to recover
slides.narration: A parser expecting malformed input should validate its lengths and return an error rather than deliberately writing beyond a buffer and hoping a signal handler can recover. A protection fault can happen after other mutations already occurred, and corrupted state may no longer support ordinary execution safely. The chapter therefore separates normal system-call error handling from attempts to repair arbitrary invalid pointer use. Our fault models use enum values and policy functions so they can be exercised safely and deterministically. When testing production code, use appropriate memory diagnostics and targeted bounds checks rather than treating a crash as the required validation path.
